articles.title: This hydrogen turbine turns controlled explosions into electricity
articles.summary: Scientists have successfully generated electricity with a hydrogen turbine that produces its own pressure through detonation waves instead of relying on a mechanical compressor. The breakthrough could unlock dramatically more efficient power systems for clean energy and future aviation.
articles.content:
Researchers at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) have achieved a major milestone in hydrogen power by operating a new compressorless gas turbine for a record 303 seconds. The burner uses an advanced form of pressure-gain combustion and surpassed NASA's previous record of 250 seconds.

The result also marks progress toward using hydrogen for cleaner energy production. Unlike natural gas, hydrogen can be produced using renewable energy sources. Earlier this year, the KIT team also became the first to generate electricity with a hydrogen gas turbine that does not rely on a mechanical compressor.

Hydrogen Turbine Runs for More Than Five Minutes

Earlier experiments could continue for only fractions of a second because longer operation would cause the combustion chambers to melt. The new test extended the operating time to more than five minutes.

"This is an important step toward highly efficient and flexible hydrogen energy for a fossil-free energy system," explains Professor Daniel Banuti, Director of the Institute of Thermal Energy Technology and Safety (ITES).

A key benefit of the design is that it does not require energy to compress air before combustion begins.

"A conventional gas turbine, such as those used in power plants or under aircraft wings, consumes about 50 percent of its power to compress air to the high pressure needed for efficient combustion -- power that is then unavailable for electricity generation," Banuti explains.

Detonation Waves Replace the Compressor

The new turbine is built around pressure-gain combustion. Conventional gas turbines use a mechanical compressor to raise air pressure, a process that can consume roughly half of the turbine's power output.

The KIT system creates the required pressure inside the combustion chamber instead. Detonation waves form through a fluid mechanical instability involving wave and vortex patterns in the flowing gases. This allows the turbine to operate without a mechanical compressor.

Removing the compressor could reduce energy losses, lower the number of moving components, and improve overall efficiency.

Why Hydrogen Works So Well

The technology can operate with fuels other than hydrogen, but hydrogen is especially suitable because it reacts very quickly and can produce stable increases in pressure.

Researchers say the approach could eventually support turbines that are lighter, less expensive, and highly efficient. Potential applications include electricity generation and, over the longer term, aviation.

Generating Electricity Without Mechanical Compression

Connecting the combustion chamber to a turbine and converting its intense combustion into electricity created an additional engineering challenge. The rapid and powerful reactions inside the chamber make it difficult to transfer energy to the turbine in a stable way.

"This is extremely difficult because the very fast and intense combustion processes in the chamber make stable energy transfer to the turbine challenging. We are the first to successfully operate such a turbine and generate electricity in the process," says Banuti.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant technological breakthrough in hydrogen turbine technology that enables more efficient, cleaner energy production by eliminating the need for mechanical compressors. This advancement has broad implications for renewable energy generation and future aviation, contributing to a fossil-free energy system with tangible environmental benefits. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights a real-world achievement with potential large-scale impact.

articles.title: Tiny patch of Amazon probably holds 40,000 insect species — many new to science
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 August 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02350-6Megaproject involving hundreds of sites is cataloguing rainforest insects from the ground to the canopy.
articles.content:
A juvenile female of the mantid species Choeradodis rhomboidea was collected as part of an effort to catalog insects in the Amazon.Credit: Bernardo Ferraz/BioInsecta

The Amazon’s lush rainforest harbours a hidden world of tiny creatures, nearly all of them unknown to science. But now hundreds of scientists in Brazil are collaborating on a quest to count every species of insect in one expanse of the Amazon — the largest insect-biodiversity study to ever explore the forest from the ground to the canopy.

Preliminary data suggest that the number of insect species could surpass 40,000, which is almost 0.7% of the widely accepted estimate of 6 million living insect species worldwide. And that 40,000 figure is for a single location in the Amazon. “If we start sampling other parts of the forest, the number of new species will likely increase almost exponentially,” says José Rafael, an entomologist at the National Institute for Amazonian Research (INPA) in Manaus, Brazil, and one of the scientists leading the megaproject.

Unpicking the rhythms of the Amazon rainforest

The project is unique, says Rudolf Meier, an entomologist at the Museum of Natural History in Berlin, because it is collecting insects high above the ground, in layers that have remained largely unexplored. He adds that the megaproject is also one of the largest to use DNA barcoding in insects, a method which identifies a species on the basis of a short fragment of its DNA, enabling researchers to sequence parts of the genome of thousands of specimens in a small amount of time.

An overview of the campaign was presented in a video poster as part of the online programme of the annual meeting of the Brazilian Society for the Advancement of Science in Niterói last week.

Stacks of traps

To collect insects, project scientists have deployed three arrays of traps. Each array consists of five mesh traps arranged in a vertical stack: one on the forest floor, one suspended about 30 metres (roughly the height of a 10-storey building) above it and three more in between. Insects that fly into each trap are funnelled into a collecting bottle at the top. There, they fall into ethanol, which kills the insects while preserving their DNA for analysis.

Researchers are deploying five-level trap systems to find insects from the forest floor to the treetops.Credit: Larissa Queiroz/BioInsecta

The trap systems, which are installed in a 10,000-hectare area of central Amazon in northern Brazil, have collected insects continuously for 14 months. To catch species that would otherwise be missed by this kind of trap, the team organized an insect-collecting ‘blitz’ last November that used around 50 extra collection methods. For example, researchers used rotting meat to attract carrion-feeding flies and beetles, as well as light traps to sample nocturnal insects.

The result was a sample of 5.5 million specimens, of which around 600,000 will ultimately have sections of their DNA sequenced. A network of nearly 400 taxonomists will combine genetic data with analyses of the insects’ physical traits to identify them. And, in the case of new species, they will describe and name them.

“Coming up with names for all of the new species is going to be a lot of work,” says Dalton Amorim, an entomologist at the University of São Paulo in Ribeirão Preto and one of the leaders of the project. Researchers might draw inspiration from words in the languages of Amazonian Indigenous groups, as well as the names of local rivers and regional historical figures, he says.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a large-scale scientific effort to catalog insect biodiversity in the Amazon rainforest, revealing potentially 40,000 species in a single location, many new to science. This has broad environmental significance for understanding and conserving biodiversity, uses innovative DNA barcoding technology, and involves extensive collaboration among hundreds of scientists, making it a substantial and inspiring environmental discovery.

articles.title: The Great Bubble Barrier: bubble curtains are intercepting 86 percent of river plastic
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Rivers are how plastic gets to the ocean. Stop it there, and you stop it for good. The Great Bubble Barrier, a Dutch company, built a technology to do exactly that. A perforated tube runs across the bed of a waterway and connects to an air pump. The pump […]
The post The Great Bubble Barrier: bubble curtains are intercepting 86 percent of river plastic first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Rivers are how plastic gets to the ocean. Stop it there, and you stop it for good. The Great Bubble Barrier, a Dutch company, built a technology to do exactly that.

A perforated tube runs across the bed of a waterway and connects to an air pump. The pump creates a rising curtain of bubbles. Installed diagonally across the river’s flow, the current naturally carries floating plastic and material suspended lower in the water column to a collection point at the bank. The system does not block fish. It does not block ship traffic. It covers the full width and depth of the river.

What it catches

Universities and independent research institutes have validated the system. It captures around 86 percent of surface plastic. “That number is indeed quite stable,” says Anne Marieke Eveleens, the company’s chief business development officer.

The Great Bubble Barrier currently operates in Amsterdam, Katwijk, and Harlingen in the Netherlands, and near Vila do Conde in Portugal. Installations in Europe and the United States are under discussion.

Why rivers matter more than beaches

Less than 10 percent of plastic is recycled globally. The rest enters waterways through poor waste management or accident. Beach clean-ups and ocean collection efforts help. They are not keeping pace.

“The production of plastic is only increasing,” Eveleens says. “We expect it to triple by 2030. The demand for plastics is very high. We use it in all of our daily activities, and at the same time, we don’t really know what to do with this plastic at the end of its life.”

Catching plastic in rivers, before it disperses into the open ocean, is a different category of problem. The Great Bubble Barrier’s 86 percent capture rate is what becomes possible when you get to it early enough.

The scaling challenge

The company’s stated ambition is Southeast Asia, where some of the world’s most heavily polluted rivers flow. Getting there is not only an engineering problem.

“You need to make sure that permits are in place, that there’s a waste collection system so that our waste doesn’t end up a few meters further into the river again,” Eveleens says. “We work together with communities in the local area, we ask their help to figure out what the most frequent object is that we find and whether we can do something about it locally.”

Every deployment requires governments, local waste managers, and communities to coordinate. Recognition through the Earthshot Prize, Prince William’s global environmental award, accelerated that effort. “Almost everywhere we go in the world, people have heard of a bubble barrier,” Eveleens says. “It really made a huge push for us to go international and bring our solution to where it’s needed.”

Beyond collection

The barrier does more than pull plastic from rivers. Every deployment generates data: what types of plastic appear most frequently, where, and when. That information feeds back into policy upstream.

“All this data that we’re gathering is also a way to make new policy to prevent it from happening in the first place,” Eveleens says.

The technology is validated. It is operating across four sites in two countries. More are under negotiation. The engineering problem is solved. Getting the barriers into every river that needs one is the work that remains.

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.

articles.personality_title: Italy develops wheat that can survive climate change for future pasta
articles.personality_presentation:
